title: How to Set Up Sony Proxy Recording for On-Set Review
summary: Learn how to enable Sony proxy recording, choose review or editorial proxy settings, transfer files from set, and relink them to original media in Premiere, Resolve, or Avid.
body_markdown:
For on-set review, turn Sony proxy recording on before the first take and treat the proxy files as review media, not as a replacement for dailies or the camera originals. The goal is simple:[record a lightweight file](https://helpguide.sony.net/pro/z200nx800/v1/en/contents/proxy_shooting.html) at the same time as the high-quality master, move that file fast, let editorial or producers start watching, and keep enough shared metadata that the proxy can be matched back to the original media later.


That decision sounds obvious until you hit the real-world details: which Sony camera, which recording format, whether you're shooting X-OCN, XAVC, ProRes, or XAVC S, whether review needs audio, whether the proxies are going to an NLE or just a browser-based review system, and whether they need to leave set before the card is even offloaded.


The clean setup is “make the smallest file that still carries the right timecode, clip identity, frame rate, audio, and visual intent for the people reviewing it.”


## How Sony proxy recording fits into the camera workflow


Sony’s proxy recording feature records a lower-resolution, lower-bitrate clip while the camera records the high-resolution original. On many current Sony cameras this happens directly in camera, so the DIT or assistant editor doesn't have to wait for post-transcode proxies before anyone can review the material.


Sony proxy recording creates a full-size original and a smaller proxy at the same time. That matters most when the original format is heavy or slow to move. VENICE and other CineAlta workflows may involve RAW, X-OCN, XAVC 4K/QFHD, ProRes, or MPEG HD depending on the body and recorder configuration.[X-OCN is designed](https://pro.sony/en_PS/insight/cinematography-tips/x-ocn-workflow-guide) to be much smaller than uncompressed RAW while preserving 16-bit scene-linear image data, and it has broad NLE and grading support, but it's still not the file you want to push over a limited network connection for fast producer review.


A proxy workflow splits the job into two tracks:


- Camera originals stay protected for archive, conform, finishing, VFX, and grade.
- Proxies move quickly to review, logging, stringouts, or offline editorial.
- Shared timecode, clip naming, reel naming, and duration allow the proxy to point back to the original.
- Looks or LUT decisions can travel with the review process when the team needs a closer representation of intent.


Proxy recording is a production workflow choice. If the camera creates proxies in camera, they can exist minutes or hours before a traditional dailies pipeline would have generated editorial media.


## Pick the proxy based on where it's going


Start with the review destination. A proxy for a director watching takes on set, a story producer screening selects remotely, and an assistant editor attaching proxies in an NLE don't need exactly the same thing.


Choose proxy settings based on where the files need to go next. Sony cameras vary in their exact proxy options, but the decision usually comes down to resolution, codec family, bitrate, audio, and whether the proxy is meant for upload while recording. Some mirrorless and compact cinema bodies offer low-bitrate XAVC S HD or[XAVC HS HD](https://helpguide.sony.net/ilc/2410/v1/en/contents/0412M_proxy_rec.html) proxy options. Some professional camcorders support proxy clips that the camera can subdivide into short chunks for upload. VENICE workflows may involve simultaneous recording combinations such as RAW/X-OCN with XAVC, or XAVC with ProRes proxy depending on firmware, media, and configuration.


For fast review, these are the tradeoffs that matter most:


- A lower bitrate transfers faster and plays more smoothly on the web, but shows more compression artifacts.
- A lower resolution is easier to upload and play back, but is less useful for focus review or detailed continuity notes.
- An edit-friendly codec is easier to attach in editorial, but may create larger files than a web-first proxy.
- Matching frame rate and timecode are essential if editorial will ever relink the file or use it for offline edit.
- Audio channel compatibility is important for transcription, dialogue review, and NLE proxy attachment.


If the proxy will only be watched for content, a small HD file is often enough. If the proxy will become editorial offline media, favor predictability over absolute size. Editors care less that a proxy is tiny and more that it links cleanly, plays consistently, and doesn't surprise them with missing audio or mismatched durations.


## Enabling simultaneous proxy recording on Sony cameras


The exact menu path changes by body, but the pattern is consistent: enable proxy recording under the project, recording, or image quality menu, choose the proxy format/settings where available, confirm the card setup, and then record normally. Proxy recording starts when the main recording starts.


On cameras using newer Sony professional menu structures, you may see proxy controls under a path like[Project, Proxy Rec, Setting](https://helpguide.sony.net/ilc/2630/v1/en/contents/proxy_shooting.html) . On some Alpha-style bodies, proxy settings may live under Shooting, Image Quality/Rec, Proxy Settings. Some models expose options for proxy file format, bitrate, color sampling, bit depth, or audio channel selection.


A typical Sony proxy setup involves these settings:


- Turn Proxy Recording or Proxy Rec Setting on.
- Select the available HD proxy format that matches the workflow destination under Proxy file format.
- Choose the bitrate and bit depth option appropriate for review or editorial under Proxy recording settings.
- Choose the channel pair or channel mapping if the camera supports audio channel control.
- Set the camera ID, reel, and naming convention before shooting.
- Confirm timecode mode and sync plan before the camera creates proxy and original files.


Don't treat these as camera-department-only settings. The assistant editor, DIT, post supervisor, or whoever owns the conform should know how the camera will name and store proxy files. A proxy that looks fine on set can still become a problem later if its clip identity doesn't map cleanly to the original.


One important compatibility note: on some Sony cameras, proxy recording can't run at the same time as certain special recording modes. For example, some help guides call out that Proxy Rec can't run simultaneously with[Slow & Quick Motion](https://helpguide.sony.net/pro/z200nx800/v1/en/contents/proxy_shooting.html) , and enabling one mode can force the other off. If the day includes off-speed work, test that exact shooting mode instead of assuming the proxy setting will stay active.


## Card setup and where the camera writes the proxy files


Sony cameras usually record proxy files alongside the main media structure, but not necessarily in the same folder as the camera originals. The camera may place them in a proxy-specific directory or under a media structure such as M4ROOT or PRIVATE, depending on body and format. Some models allow the root folder naming to follow a camera ID and reel pattern, which can help the post team keep multi-camera days sane.


On certain Sony professional camcorders, the camera derives proxy file names from the original clip name with a suffix such as S03. For chunked upload workflows, the proxy may include the original clip name plus a chunk number and suffix. The camera records timecode simultaneously, which is the key piece that lets review media stay useful beyond simple playback.


During prep, confirm whether the file carries the right relationship to the original. Shoot a short test, offload both the original and proxy, and inspect the results in the same toolchain the production will use. That means the NLE, the review system, the cloud upload process, or the media management app, not only the camera playback screen.


Test the full path by offloading both media types and checking them in the real workflow. A few details deserve attention during that test:


- File extension and wrapper, such as MP4 or mp4 depending on proxy format.
- Folder path, especially if automated ingest expects a specific structure.
- Clip name relationship between proxy and original.
- Timecode start, duration, and frame rate.
- Audio channel count and channel order.
- Card access behavior before removing media or powering down.


The last point is about card handling, but it matters, so if the camera is writing proxy media and original media, wait for card access indicators before pulling cards or shutting down. Losing a small proxy is annoying, but risking the integrity of the recording media is worse.


## Getting proxies off set quickly


There are two common ways to move Sony proxies for fast review: copy them during normal media offload, or push them automatically through a network workflow.


Transfer method Best fit How it works Main advantage Watch point


Supervised card offload Scripted work, commercials, and controlled media workflows The DIT or data manager copies camera originals with checksum verification, extracts or copies proxies, then sends the proxy folder to review or editorial Strong media control and clear accountability Proxies usually move after the card reaches the offload station


Proxy auto-upload News, documentary, field production, and remote producer review The camera uploads proxy files to a configured FTP server or supported cloud destination Review media can leave set before full camera originals arrive Network setup, authentication, and upload failures need active monitoring


Selected or chunked transfer Fast turnaround review when only part of a clip is needed The workflow transfers selected clips, selected ranges, or short proxy segments while recording continues Smaller transfers can arrive sooner than full-take proxies Spanned or chunked files can complicate duration checks and NLE relinking


The normal offload method is safer and easier to supervise. The camera card comes to the DIT or data manager, the DIT or data manager copies originals with checksum verification, copies or extracts proxies from the card structure, and then sends the proxy folder to review or editorial. This is usually the right approach for commercials, scripted work, and any shoot where media control matters more than shaving off a few minutes.


The faster method is proxy auto-upload. Some Sony professional camera and camcorder workflows allow cameras to upload proxies automatically to an FTP server or supported cloud destination. Some workflows also support browsing proxy clip lists remotely, selecting clips or portions of clips, and transferring only the selected range. Chunked proxy upload can subdivide a clip into short segments so transfer can begin before the full recording has finished.


That gives production a few useful patterns:


- Field producers can review proxies that upload automatically from camera or the camera operator's location.
- Assistant editors can receive lightweight files before full camera originals arrive.
- News or documentary teams can transfer selected parts of a clip first instead of the whole take.
- Production offices can receive proxies throughout the day while camera originals remain on set.


The tradeoff is reliability and control. Auto-upload depends on network quality, authentication, destination setup, and whether the camera operator can afford to manage failures during production. For a high-pressure set, preconfigure the destination, test with the actual cards and camera settings, and make the upload status visible to someone other than the camera operator if possible.


## Review proxies still need a look


A proxy that's technically correct but visually misleading can create bad notes. If the director, DP, client, or producer is reviewing a flat log-looking proxy without knowing it, you can lose time explaining exposure, contrast, or color that would look normal with the intended monitoring LUT.


Sony workflows often include on-set look management, including LUTs for monitoring and review.[Sony’s s709 look](https://sony-cinematography.com/venice-2-and-burano-cinealta-workflow-guide/) , for example, is designed for on-set monitoring and clip review, with a film-like contrast and color response. VENICE and FX9-style workflows commonly use LUTs or ART files as part of the production’s viewing pipeline.


The decision here is whether the proxy should represent the technical capture or the intended viewing transform. For editorial and conform, the original media and metadata matter most. For client review, continuity, and performance notes, a reasonable viewing look is often more useful. Your team can mix those two purposes without labeling them.


If your proxy review path applies a LUT, make that clear in the naming, burn-in, metadata, or review notes. If it doesn't apply a LUT, make sure reviewers know they're seeing log or a technical image. Don't let “proxy” become a mystery file where nobody knows whether the look is baked, displayed, or absent.


## Using Catalyst Browse in the handoff


Sony Catalyst Browse is useful when the team needs a Sony-aware way to inspect, copy, log, and transcode media. It can browse files from Sony cameras, show detailed clip information, copy media to local storage, and transcode to other formats.


For proxy workflows, Catalyst Browse isn't automatically required, but it's a good sanity tool. If a proxy file isn't appearing where expected, if your team needs to inspect metadata, or if the production wants to export a different review format from Sony source media, it can help bridge camera and post.


Use it during prep and troubleshooting, and confirm that Catalyst Browse sees the clips as expected, that the camera-original media is intact, and that any proxy or transcode files line up with the clip metadata post expects. Then decide whether Catalyst is part of the daily process or just a support tool.


## Relinking proxies to original media in the NLE


Relinking depends on the NLE, but the matching logic is always some combination of filename, reel or tape name, source timecode, duration, frame rate, and audio structure. In-camera proxies make this easier when they preserve timecode and maintain a predictable naming relationship to the original clips.


Relinking works when proxy and source clips share matching identity and technical properties. In Premiere Pro, a typical flow is to import or ingest the original camera media,[attach proxies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VaEND8gpKR4) , and toggle proxy playback while keeping the originals online for export. In DaVinci Resolve, editors may use proxy media, optimized media, or camera originals directly depending on codec support and machine performance. In Avid Media Composer, assistant editors often care deeply about source clip metadata, tape/reel naming, and whether proxies were generated or linked in a way that supports conform.


Before committing to in-camera proxies as editorial media, test the NLE with the exact camera settings. Watch for these relink problems:


- Proxy and original filenames differ in a way the NLE can't automatically associate.
- Timecode matches, but reel or source name is missing or inconsistent.
- Proxy frame rate doesn't match the original.
- Proxy duration differs because of spanned clips, chunked uploads, or interrupted recording.
- Audio channel count differs between proxy and original, causing attach or relink failures.
- A flattened proxy folder structure lost context needed for ingest.


The most common preventable mistake is renaming or reorganizing proxy files by hand before editorial receives them. If you need human-readable folders, create folders around the camera structure rather than modifying the files inside it. Keep camera card copies intact, keep proxy exports traceable, and document any transform between original and review media.


## Where in-camera proxies aren't enough


In-camera proxies are great for speed, but they aren't the answer to every post workflow. Production may still need a proper dailies pipeline when review files require burn-ins, synced double-system audio, CDL or LUT application, watermarking, scene/take metadata, multiple deliverable formats, or editorial codecs that differ from the camera’s proxy options.


Sony’s own CineAlta workflow framing separates on-set look management, data transfer and backup, dailies, and editorial. Proxy recording can speed up several of those stages, but it doesn't replace all of them. If editorial needs synced audio and ALE metadata, camera proxies alone may only be a temporary review asset. If finishing will conform from X-OCN or RAW, the proxy’s real value is speed and reference, not final image quality.


A good rule: use camera proxies for immediate access, and use dailies or post-generated proxies when the file needs to carry more editorial structure than the camera can create.


## A clean Sony proxy setup in practice


After the test clip is open in the review tool and the NLE, confirm the handoff details that will affect the workflow:


- timecode
- clip naming
- frame rate
- audio
- relink behavior


Once that's working, protect the pattern. Don't change clip naming halfway through a shoot day. Don't let different cameras use conflicting camera IDs or reel names. Don't flatten card structures unless post has approved that ingest method. If proxy auto-upload is part of the workflow, test the destination and failure recovery before the first real take.


Sony’s proxy recording is valuable because it moves review earlier in the day. The camera can create lightweight media while preserving the high-quality original path, whether that original is XAVC, ProRes, RAW, or X-OCN. The setup only works if production treats the proxy as part of the media chain from the start, with the same discipline around naming, timecode, audio, and handoff that they already apply to the camera originals.


## FAQ


Usually no. Sony in-camera proxies are best for fast review, logging, remote viewing, or early offline access. A full dailies workflow may still be needed for synced double-system audio, burn-ins, LUT or CDL application, watermarking, scene and take metadata, editorial deliverables, and quality control.


Choose the smallest proxy that still preserves the information your workflow needs: matching frame rate, source timecode, usable audio, predictable clip names, and enough image quality for review. For simple producer or client viewing, a low-bitrate HD proxy is often enough. For editorial offline work, prioritize NLE compatibility and clean relinking over the smallest possible file size.


The location depends on the camera model and recording format. Sony proxies may be stored in a proxy-specific folder or inside a camera media structure such as PRIVATE or M4ROOT. During prep, shoot a test clip and confirm the proxy folder path, filename relationship, timecode, duration, audio channels, and how the files appear in the review system or NLE.


Not always. Some Sony cameras don't allow proxy recording at the same time as certain special recording modes, including Slow & Quick Motion on some models. Test the exact camera, firmware, codec, frame rate, and recording mode before the shoot so the crew knows when proxy recording will remain active and when it may be disabled.


Relinking usually depends on a combination of filename, source timecode, reel or tape name, duration, frame rate, and audio structure. In-camera proxies are easier to attach when they preserve timecode and maintain a predictable naming relationship to the originals. Avoid renaming proxy files or flattening camera folders unless post has approved that method.


Treat the in-camera Sony proxies as the review asset and keep the originals in the controlled media path. Aspect lets teams upload those lightweight files for frame-accurate comments, annotations, replies, and approvals in a shared review workflow.
